title: Mexican Manufacturing Output Under Alternative Import Paths: Fixed-Point Local Projections for Conditional Forecasting
content: When economic variables operate in a closed loop of bilateral feedback ($M_t \leftrightarrow Y_t$), conditional forecasting encounters a fundamental methodological dilemma. Imposing an externally specified future trajectory on one endogenous variable while allowing the second to respond alters the first variable through reverse feedback, breaking dynamic consistency. Conversely, treating the conditioning path as an exogenous driver throughout the forecast horizon suppresses the reverse feedback channel and conflates direct impulse transmission with cumulative system-wide interaction. This paper develops an Iterative Alternating Proxy (IAP) computational framework—Fixed-Point Local Projections (FP-LP) with an Error-Correction Mechanism (ECM)—for conditional forecasting and model-based scenario analysis under bilateral feedback, without claiming closed-form structural identification or new asymptotic distribution theory for the over-identified Huber-IAP estimator. At each horizon h, the procedure embeds two-equation local projections within an alternating Gauss–Seidel updating loop, iteratively re-estimating generated fitted proxies until mutual numerical consistency is attained conditional on maintained within-system exclusion restrictions. Crucially, the methodology yields an exact model-based three-way response decomposition ($R_h^{FP} = R_h^{SP} + \Delta R_h^{Norm} + \Delta R_h^{Iter}$) that separates the converged cumulative fixed-point trajectory from a restricted single-pass impulse benchmark ($R_h^{SP}$) into a cumulative proxy normalization shift ($\Delta R_h^{Norm}$) and iterative feedback updating ($\Delta R_h^{Iter}$). Deploying the Mexican manufacturing sector (2011:01–2025:12) as an empirical application, the decomposition shows that the 66.9% reduction at h=12 relative to the single-pass impulse projection is primarily a normalization shift from one-month impulse scaling to cumulative import-path scaling ($\Delta R_{12}^{Norm} = -0.6924$), whereas iterative feedback updating ($\Delta R_{12}^{Iter} = +0.0069$, peaking at +0.0664 at $h=21$) contributes much less. At long horizons (h>24), raw local projection estimates become noisy ($\hat{\gamma}_{1,36} = -0.7923, \text{SE} = 1.385$), so the FP-SLP terminal trajectory (+0.2004 at h=36, versus −0.4617 without boundary penalties) reflects an imposed DOLS long-run boundary condition ($\theta_M^{LR} = 0.2014$) rather than empirically discovered convergence. In the 36-month scenario exercise (which extends beyond the 12-month out-of-sample validation horizon), a 12-month import restriction generates cumulative output losses 3.64 times those of a 3-month restriction of the same monthly magnitude; because a static constant-multiplier benchmark already produces a mechanical ratio of 3.50, the additional +0.14 difference is small and does not constitute strong evidence of dynamic amplification, while absolute cumulative losses remain sensitive to sample period and cointegration rank. Finally, recursive out-of-sample evaluation across 36 holdout origins at horizons of 1, 3, 6, and 12 months detects no statistically significant differences in expected squared-error loss relative to the naive random walk benchmark.
